title: Khanate of Kazan
wiki_lead:
The Khanate of Kazan, also called the Kazan Khanate, was a Tatar state on the Middle Volga, in the territory of the former Volga Bulgaria, from the mid-15th century until 1552. It covered present-day Tatarstan, Mari El, Chuvashia, Mordovia, and parts of Udmurtia and Bashkortostan; its capital was Kazan.
The khanate was one of the successor states of the Golden Horde. Historians date its founding either to 1437 or 1438, when Ulugh Muhammad took power in Kazan, or to 1445, when his son Maxmud began to rule there. Its history was marked by frequent changes of khan and by conflict between pro-Moscow and pro-Crimean groups in the nobility. From 1487 to 1521 the khanate was in effect a Muscovite protectorate. The Tsardom of Russia conquered it in 1552, after the siege of Kazan, and resistance in the former khanate continued until 1557.
The population included Tatars, Chuvash, Mari, Mordvins, Udmurts, and Bashkirs. Sunni Islam was the state religion. The khan was formally the sole ruler, but real power lay with the diwan, an assembly of the highest religious and secular aristocracy. The towns lived by crafts and by trade with Russia, Central Asia, and the Caucasus, and the Taşayaq fair in Kazan was the main fair of the Volga region.

Geography and population
The territory of the khanate comprised the Muslim Bulgar-populated lands of the Bolğar, Cükätäw, Kazan, and Qaşan duchies and other regions that originally belonged to Volga Bulgaria. The Volga, Kama, and Vyatka were the main rivers of the khanate, as well as the major trade routes. The size of the Tatar population is disputed. The Chuvash encyclopedia describes the Tatars as a minority that formed the ruling class, and gives the tribute-paying Chuvash, about 200,000 people, as the largest group. Most of the population identified itself by religion, as Muslims, and people also called themselves "the people of Kazan" (qazanlılar). Sunni Islam of the Hanafi school was the state religion.
The local feudal nobility consisted of ethnic Bulgars, but the court and bodyguard of the Kazan khans were composed of steppe Tatars (Kipchaks, and later Nogais) who lived in Kazan. According to the Genghisid tradition, the local Turkic tribes were also called Tatars by the steppe nobility and, later, by the Russian elite. The highest nobility came from four ruling clans: Shirin, Barin, Arghin, and Qipchaq. In the 1540s and 1550s the Manghit clan was added to them.
Peoples subject to the khan included the Chuvash, Mari, Mordvins, Udmurts, and Bashkirs. Mishar Tatars and some Komi tribes also lived in the khanate. The Mishars had arrived during the period of the Golden Horde and gradually assimilated the resident Mordvins and Burtas. Their territory was governed by former steppe Tatars. Some Mishar duchies were never controlled from Kazan and instead gravitated toward the Qasim Khanate or Muscovite Russia.
Most of the khanate territory was covered by forests, and only the southern part adjoined the steppe. The main population of the steppes were the nomadic Manghites, also known as Nogais, who sometimes recognized the rule of the Kazan khan, but more often raided agricultural Tatars and Chuvash, as they had done in the Golden Horde period. Later, Nogais were transplanted and replaced with Kalmyks. More recently, this area was settled by Tatars, Chuvash, and Russians, who erected defensive walls to guard the southern border. Since the khanate was established, Tatar Cossack troops defended the khanate from the Nogais.
The most widely spoken language, and the official language, was Volga Turki (Old Tatar), which was used in administration and diplomatic correspondence. Prince Andrey Kurbsky wrote that five other languages were spoken in the khanate besides Tatar: Mordvin, Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt, and Bashkir. The Chuvash language was a descendant of the Bulgar language, which also strongly influenced the Middle dialect of the Tatar language.

grok_lead: The Khanate of Kazan was a Tatar khanate founded in 1438 by Ulugh Muhammad, a prince of the Golden Horde, who established control over the former Volga Bulgaria with Kazan as its capital. It represented one of the primary successor states to the disintegrating Golden Horde, encompassing territories along the middle Volga River that included modern-day Tatarstan and adjacent regions inhabited by Turkic Tatars and Finno-Ugric groups such as the Chuvash and Mari. Ruled by Muslim khans primarily from the Jochid lineage, the khanate developed as a commercial hub facilitating trade between Europe and Central Asia via the Volga River, while sustaining an economy based on agriculture, craftsmanship, and tribute extraction from subject peoples. Its relations with the rising Grand Duchy of Moscow were marked by intermittent warfare, including raids and defensive campaigns that escalated over the 15th and 16th centuries, reflecting competition for regional dominance and resources. The khanate's internal instability, characterized by succession disputes and alliances with the Crimean Khanate or Nogai Horde, ultimately facilitated its conquest by Tsar Ivan IV in 1552, an event that initiated Muscovite expansion into the Volga basin and beyond, incorporating diverse non-Slavic populations under Russian suzerainty. This annexation not only secured vital trade arteries but also provided Moscow with strategic access to Siberia, reshaping Eurasian power dynamics through direct military subjugation rather than mere tributary relations.
